executive_summary: USD/CHF closed at 0.82432 on 30 October. The pair is quoted in francs per dollar, so a rising pair means a stronger dollar. It is 0.81% lower over one month but 1.91% higher over three months, 5.59% higher over six and 3.33% higher over a year, which puts it at the 84th percentile of its 52-week closing range of 0.76602-0.83581. The pair is a carry trade meeting a safe haven. The Fed's 3.875% mid-point against the SNB's 0% is a 387.5bp gap, and unlike the dollar's spreads to the euro, yen, Canadian dollar and krona, it is not narrowing. A rolled long collects the listed franc futures premium of about 449bp a year, roughly 31 pips a month. The two standalone dossiers are Bullish on the dollar and Neutral on the franc tactically. Read together, they reinforce each other, because the franc is weakest exactly where the dollar is strongest: rates and funding. The forces that could unwind the trade are the franc's haven role, the largest leveraged franc short since May and the risk of US action on Iran after the midterms. The tactical stance is Bullish, conviction 2 (score +0.154). The base case is 0.8340 by 27 November, with a stop on a daily close below 0.8145. The strategic stance is Bearish, conviction 2 (score -0.222). The base case is 0.7980 by end-April 2027, as twin US deficits against a large Swiss surplus and the back-to-back December projection rounds narrow the expected gap. The chart fits that firm-then-fade path. Spot is above its 50-, 100- and 200-day averages but 298 pips below a 200-week average that falls 7.7 pips a week and will reach the five-touch 0.8375-0.8456 resistance band by mid-January. The caveat is carry: the six-month forward of 0.8058 already discounts 2.24% of decline, so a short opened at today's spot has close to zero expected value after carry. The strategic view is better built from 0.8300-0.8350 after the 9-10 December decisions, or through options.

market_context.valuation_assessment: On GDP-based PPP the franc is about 12.9% rich against the dollar, which equals a dollar about 11.4% cheap on the US dossier's convention, implying fair value near 0.9307, 1,064 pips above spot. That premium has persisted for decades on the back of Switzerland's 5-10%-of-GDP current account surplus and does not mean-revert inside six months. In real effective terms both legs are cheap against their own recent history. The BIS real broad index for Switzerland is 98.37, the lowest of 33 monthly readings since January 2024 and 4.60 points lower over a year. The US index is 107.11, the 21st percentile of the same window. Bilaterally the real-rate picture is close to balanced, slightly favouring the franc, which has cheapened more. The current level prices the 387.5bp carry gap continuing, but not a Swiss surplus reasserting itself once peer hiking cycles end.

market_context.recent_regime: The pair spent June to September as a franc-funded carry trade. The SNB held at zero while every major peer except Norges Bank hiked or prepared to, and the Fed's 16 September hike added 71 pips in a session. The SNB said the franc's fall was in line with widened rate differentials, which together with low volatility made it a more attractive carry-trade funding currency, with little safe-haven demand since June. October broke that pattern against the euro more than against the dollar. A French sovereign spread above 150bp pulled haven money into francs, and the pair fell from 0.8358 to 0.8207 at the 22 October close. Into the Fed it recovered: the pair was on the front foot for a fourth consecutive day as traders favoured higher-yielding currencies, before slipping on the 30 October equity sell-off. The dominant narrative is now the question of which wins between carry and haven, and both sides are measurable.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The policy carry is 387.5bp: the Fed target mid-point of 3.875% against the SNB's 0%, both as of 27 October. This is the widest gap the dollar holds over any G10 currency. A rolled position actually earns the annualised premium between the December 2026 and March 2027 CME Swiss franc futures, 448.7bp observed on 29 October (quoted as -448.7bp on the franc futures). That premium combines the interest differential with any cross-currency basis, and the two cannot be separated without an OIS curve. On three-month implied volatility of 6.598% the carry-to-vol ratio is 0.59 on policy carry and 0.68 on the futures premium. For a long-dollar position that is the best ratio among the major dollar pairs, against roughly 0.23 for EUR/USD and 0.37 for USD/JPY. Carry is working: the pair is up 5.59% over six months while collecting it. It is also fragile, because a funding currency that is the G10's main haven can erase a quarter's carry in a day, as the 152-pip fall on 19 August showed. At the 448.7bp premium a long accrues about 31 pips a month, 92 pips over three months and 185 pips over six months at 0.82432. Those are the breakeven falls (0.37%, 1.12% and 2.24%) before the carry is erased.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the widest policy gap the dollar holds over any G10 currency. As of 27 October the Fed target mid-point was 3.875% and the SNB rate 0%, a 387.5bp differential. At the end of October the US 2-year yielded 4.61% and the Swiss 2-year 0.18%, about 443bp apart. The trajectory is unusual for a dollar pair. In October the dollar's front-end premium narrowed against the euro, yen, Canadian dollar and krona as those banks turned hawkish. The SNB is the one major peer that is not tightening, so this gap is holding rather than shrinking. Neither bank decides on policy in the next four weeks. The next repricing points are the FOMC on 9 December, with new projections, and the SNB assessment on 10 December. Until then the differential moves only through how November data shift December pricing. US payrolls on 6 November and CPI on 10 November are more likely to keep the 77-85% December hike probability in place than to remove it. Swiss October CPI on 3 November would need a large upside surprise to bring an SNB move into view. The channel is carry: a rolled long position earns the listed-futures premium of about 449bp a year, roughly 31 pips a month, and nothing is scheduled to stop that accruing before December.

tactical.what_is_priced: A December Fed hike is 77-85% priced. The SNB is priced to hold, with only about 6bp of tightening. The edge over four weeks is the carry itself, not a pricing error: the differential has no scheduled way to narrow before the 9-10 December decisions.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the question is whether the 387.5bp gap widens to 412.5bp or starts to narrow. Both answers arrive within 24 hours: the FOMC decides with projections on 9 December and the SNB publishes its assessment and new conditional forecast on 10 December. A Fed hike plus an SNB hold would widen the differential by 25bp. That is the consensus outcome and it is largely priced. What is not settled is the path beyond December. Futures price the Fed near 4.7% by September 2027 against a median dot of 4.1%, so the bigger repricing risk on the dollar side is lower. On the franc side, the SNB raised its inflation forecasts in September to 0.7% for 2026 and 0.8% for 2027 and 2028, and Bloomberg Economics sees a possible first hike in early 2027. Both surprises, measured against current pricing, would narrow the expected differential. Neither is large enough to erase a gap of nearly 400bp. And forwards already discount about 4.5% a year of franc appreciation. A wide, stable gap whose surprise risks lean towards narrowing, and whose value is already in the forward, nets to Neutral.

Strategically, the back-to-back decisions on 9 and 10 December reset both policy paths. The surprise risk on both sides points towards a narrower expected gap than is priced, and the forward already pays for the carry, so the stance moves to Neutral.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: No dollar pair has a wider inflation differential. In September US headline CPI was 3.7% and core PCE 3.1%, against Swiss CPI of 1.0% and core of 0.5%. That gap of roughly 260-270bp is what keeps the Fed hawkish and the SNB at zero. Growth momentum also favours the dollar. US third-quarter GDP rose 3.4% annualised, with real final sales to private domestic purchasers up 4.9%. Swiss momentum is fading after a pharma-driven second quarter: the KOF barometer fell to 107.6 in October and the procure.ch PMI dropped to 55.3 from 57.1. US releases move the pair more, because they shift December Fed pricing. Swiss CPI on 3 November would have to print well above 1.2% to change SNB pricing much. The US weak spot is employment. September payrolls rose only 29,000, with 60,000 of downward revisions, so the 6 November report is the main downside risk. Price surveys point to a firm CPI print on 10 November. Overall, the near-term data calendar leans towards confirming the differential.

SECO now forecasts Swiss growth of 1.7% for 2026 and 1.6% for 2027, close to the slowing US pace. Converging inflation is what narrows expected policy gaps, so this factor's strategic signal is weaker than its levels suggest. The US still runs hotter on both inflation and growth, but the direction of change favours the franc. We net the two to Neutral.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: USD/CHF sets the G10's most reliable haven against a dollar whose haven role is currently impaired. Risk appetite turned cautious at the end of October. The VIX rose to 17.2 on 29 October and traded near 20 intraday on 30 October as technology earnings hit the Nasdaq. US investment-grade spreads widened to 89bp and high yield to 326bp, the 96th and 95th percentiles of a year. On that sell-off the dollar index slipped rather than rallied, and the franc and yen took the haven demand. That fits ING's warning that low hedge ratios on US assets make a US-led risk-off dollar-negative. The two live geopolitical tails both have a record of drawing money into francs: possible US strikes on Iran after the midterms, and European sovereign stress with the OAT-Bund spread above 150bp. The SNB intervened at the start of the Iran war to stop a rush into the franc. The most likely form of risk-off is a US-centred equity wobble, so this factor points to a lower pair over four weeks.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the risk channel cuts both ways for this pair. A deeper AI-led equity correction would hit US assets first and probably raise hedge ratios on them. Combined with the franc's haven pull, that would lower the pair. A prolonged Gulf escalation would also favour the franc as a haven, but higher oil improves US terms of trade and lifts global rates, which helps the high-carry dollar against a zero-rate funder once volatility settles. Calm markets favour the other side. The SNB said in its September discussion that haven demand for the franc had been limited and that low volatility made it attractive for carry funding, and US equities remain about 11% higher over a year. A US-Iran settlement would remove the haven bid and restore franc-funded carry. Because the outcomes are roughly balanced and partly correlated, we do not take a strategic view through this factor.

The speculative franc short is not at the roughly 30,000-contract scale that has preceded past squeezes, so crowding alone is not decisive at this horizon. The asset-manager franc short is a structural hedge position that could rebuild if European stress fades. The SNB has stepped back from intervening, buying only CHF 1.437bn of foreign currency in the second quarter, so no official seller of francs is offsetting these flows. The balance is a mild bearish signal.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The external gap between the two economies is about as wide as it gets in G10. The US current account deficit widened to 3.0% of GDP in the second quarter and its investment position to -USD 22.42tn. Switzerland ran a CHF 23.7bn second-quarter surplus, about 9.2% of GDP, with a positive net position of CHF 986bn. Bilaterally, IMF DOTS shows Swiss goods exports to the US of USD 73.5bn against imports of USD 29.3bn in 2024. The US records a USD 38.6bn goods deficit with Switzerland, settled at a 15% US tariff on Swiss goods and patented pharmaceuticals. Over four weeks these are slow-moving stocks, not flows that set the pair. Near-term terms of trade lean the other way. The US is a net energy exporter with Brent at US$117.64. Switzerland is an energy importer, though energy is only about 3.5% of its CPI basket. Gold, the franc's relevant commodity, fell about 7% in October. The near-term commodity tilt offsets the structural surplus, so the factor is Neutral tactically.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the external balance is the clearest structural force pushing the pair lower. The US deficit is widening: the September advance goods deficit was USD 134.9bn, and the investment position lost USD 1.15tn in a single quarter. That deficit is financed comfortably only while US yields stay 4.6-5.0% and the rate lead holds. Switzerland's surplus produces a steady stream of foreign-currency income that must be recycled or converted. Its real effective rate fell to 98.37 in September, the lowest of 33 monthly readings, so competitiveness is not eroding the surplus. The 15% tariff settlement and pharma waivers for US investment until 2029 lower the risk of another export collapse. Valuation is the offset: on GDP-based PPP the franc is about 12-13% expensive against the dollar, a premium it has carried for decades. Twin US deficits against a large Swiss surplus, with the rate lead that finances them no longer widening against most peers, tilt this factor Bearish.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: The US is a net energy exporter. Higher oil improves its terms of trade against importers, mild +USD. Henry Hub gas at US$2.76 insulates US industry from the global energy shock.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: Switzerland is an energy importer with a small energy share of CPI (about 3.5%), so oil up is mildly -CHF. Gold up is +CHF through the haven correlation, and gold merchanting flows run through the Swiss balance of payments.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Oil up: USD gets a mild positive (+) as a net exporter, and CHF a mild negative (-) as a small-share importer. In isolation the net effect is mildly Bullish for the pair. Gold up: under the direction rules CHF gets a positive (+) and USD has no direct exposure, so the net is mildly Bearish. In October oil rose about 15% and gold fell about 7%, so both commodity channels leaned slightly towards a higher pair. The caveat is that the current oil rise is driven by the Gulf conflict. Geopolitically driven oil spikes usually come with haven demand for the franc, which outweighs the small terms-of-trade effect.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: A supply-driven 10% rise from economic strength is mildly Bullish through US terms of trade. A 10% rise from Gulf escalation is net Bearish, because haven demand for the franc outweighs the terms-of-trade gain.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: A 10% fall from a US-Iran settlement is mildly Bullish. The haven bid for the franc fades and franc-funded carry rebuilds, outweighing the small loss of US terms of trade.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Oil through its geopolitical channel rather than its trade channel, with gold as a secondary haven signal.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two banks are signalling differently in substance but not in a way that moves the pair over four weeks. The Fed's 28 October statement was hawkish: inflation 'remains elevated' and the Committee 'will deliver price stability', with Cook and Hammack dissenting for an immediate hike. But Chair Warsh declined to pre-judge December and rejected forward guidance outside a crisis. The SNB's 22 October summary of deliberations dropped the view that an increased willingness to intervene was needed, which removes a cap on franc strength. On 8 October Chair Schlegel said inflation was comfortably within the 0-2% range and saw no need to adjust policy. The only scheduled communication in the window is the FOMC minutes on 18 November, which could show a hawkish majority beyond the two dissents. The SNB is silent until 10 December. A possibly hawkish Fed minutes release against a softer SNB intervention stance roughly cancels out.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months both banks issue new forecasts within a day of each other, and the guidance risk leans against the pair. The Fed's 9 December projections are the first under a chair who rejects forward guidance. With the market already pricing a path near 4.7% for late 2027 against a 4.1% median dot, a hike-and-hold signal would be a dovish surprise relative to pricing. The SNB's 10 December conditional forecast follows a September revision that raised 2027-2028 inflation to 0.8% on oil and the weaker franc. Another upward drift would weaken the case for a permanent zero rate while every peer except Norges Bank tightens. The SNB has also stepped back from its intervention backstop and has pledged not to intervene for competitive advantage, which raises the bar for selling francs. Fed credibility is high, but the asymmetry in communication surprises favours the franc.

Strategically, the 9-10 December projection rounds are where the asymmetry shows: a dovish surprise relative to Fed pricing and a hawkish drift from the SNB. The stance moves to Bearish.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The four-week event map is heavier on the dollar side, and most of the tails point to a lower pair. The 3 November midterms are largely priced, with prediction markets at 94% for a Democratic House and 70% for a sweep. ING warns that a Republican loss of the House could push the administration back towards trade actions, which it sees as dollar-negative. The President has said the US would not strike Iran before the midterms, which leaves the period after 3 November open. Two tankers were hit in Hormuz on 29-30 October, and we put a US strike within four weeks at about 20%. An escalation would most likely send haven flows into francs, as at the war's outbreak in March, rather than into dollars. Swiss event risk is low: the 29 November federal votes are not macro-relevant. A US-Iran deal, about 15% within four weeks, is the main event that would lift the pair. The skew of outcomes is Bearish.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the event distribution is two-sided. US fiscal deadlines come back with the expiry of government funding on 11 December, and a divided Congress from January raises the chance of budget confrontations. Both would weigh on the dollar through risk premia. Renewed trade actions after the midterms could hit Swiss exports again despite the 15% settlement, but they could also undermine confidence in US assets, so the pair effect is ambiguous. In the Gulf, a settlement (about 25% within six months) would remove the haven bid for the franc and restore franc-funded carry, lifting the pair. A sustained Hormuz closure (about 15%) would do the opposite. European sovereign stress mainly affects the euro-franc cross, but it keeps haven demand alive. These branches offset each other, so the factor is Neutral.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: No G10 pair has a wider fiscal gap between its legs. The US ran a USD 2.0tn deficit in FY2026, 6.2% of GDP, with debt held by the public around 100% of GDP and interest costs at 3.4% of GDP. It is rated AA+ by S&P with a stable outlook. Switzerland is AAA/Aaa with stable outlooks, gross government debt of about 38% of GDP and a federal surplus in 2025 under the constitutional debt brake. Over four weeks, though, there is no fiscal deadline to bring the gap into play. Treasury's 4 November refunding is expected to leave coupon sizes unchanged, and the 11 December funding expiry falls just after the window. Rising Swiss bond prices in October show haven buying, but that was driven by French stress rather than US fiscal concern. The factor is Neutral tactically.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the fiscal gap becomes a live, if slow, drag on the pair. The 11 December expiry of the continuing resolution falls in a lame-duck Congress, two days after the FOMC. A lapse would delay data and raise risk premia on US assets. A Democratic House from January makes 2027 budget fights more likely. S&P has said the US rating could slip within two years if deficits rise. The long end is already charging for this, with the 30-year near 5.3% and 10-year breakevens only 2.34%, so the premium is for term and fiscal risk rather than inflation. So far higher term premia have helped the dollar by raising yields. Once the Fed stops hiking, a fiscal premium without matching policy expectations tends to weaken the currency. Switzerland faces only small structural deficits of below 0.5% of GDP. The widening differential tilts the factor Bearish.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar liquidity is tightening at the margin into month-end and year-end, while franc funding stays abundant at a 0% SNB rate. Reserve balances fell USD 68.8bn in the week to 28 October to a USD 2,893.8bn average, because the Treasury General Account rose to about USD 1tn ahead of an USD 850bn end-December target. SOFR printed 3.94% on 29 October, 4bp above interest on reserve balances. Reserve management purchases have been zero since mid-August, and the standing repo facility and swap lines are barely used, so there is tightness but no stress. The annualised premium between listed Swiss franc futures is 448.7bp, about 61bp more than the policy differential. That excess mixes expected Fed hikes with any franc basis and cannot be split without an OIS curve, so we do not read it as a dollar shortage. Firming dollar funding costs against a franc that remains the cheapest major funder support the pair over four weeks.

The Desk is authorised to buy bills and short coupons to keep reserves ample, and reserve management purchases have a tested record. Treasury's planned fall in the General Account to USD 850bn by end-December would return about USD 165bn of reserves, easing conditions in early 2027. On the franc side, SNB sight deposits are stable and the SNB pays 0.25pp less on balances above the threshold, which keeps Swiss money-market rates slightly below zero-policy levels and the franc cheap to borrow. Year-end tightness that is met by renewed bill purchases, followed by a falling Treasury cash balance, leaves no persistent dollar-funding signal for this pair.

tactical.score_interpretation: A net score of +0.154 clears the +0.10 threshold, so the tactical stance is Bullish: USD/CHF is expected to rise over four weeks. The score rests on depth in three heavily weighted factors: Policy & Rates (+0.134), Inflation & Growth (+0.095) and USD Liquidity (+0.057). Against them is a breadth of three lighter franc-positive factors: Risk Appetite (-0.054), Flows & Positioning (-0.053) and Event Risk (-0.026). The dollar's carry and data advantages do the work. The opposing factors all describe the same single risk, a haven-driven unwind of a crowded carry trade.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights, Policy & Rates (0.24), Inflation & Growth (0.18) and USD Liquidity (0.11) carry more than half the score, and all three point to a higher pair. The Fed mid-point of 3.875% against the SNB's 0% is a 387.5bp gap, the widest the dollar holds in G10. Unlike the dollar's gaps with the euro, yen and krona, it is not narrowing, because the SNB is the one major bank not tightening. US CPI at 3.7% and core PCE at 3.1%, against Swiss CPI of 1.0% and core of 0.5%, keep that gap anchored. US releases on 6 and 10 November matter more for the pair than Swiss CPI on 3 November. Dollar funding is firming as reserves fall below USD 2.9tn. Together these produce +0.287. Against them, the franc's haven role, a crowded fast-money long and post-midterm Iran risk subtract 0.133, leaving +0.154: Bullish at conviction 2. The base dossier is Bullish on the dollar and the quote dossier Neutral on the franc. Combined bilaterally, they reinforce each other, because the franc is weak exactly where the dollar is strong: on rates and funding. What is priced is a December Fed hike at 77-85% and an SNB hold. The edge is not a mispricing but carry of about 31 pips a month, with no scheduled decision from either bank until 9 and 10 December to disturb it. The path of least resistance over four weeks is a carry-supported drift higher, interrupted by haven episodes. The dated catalysts are Swiss CPI and the midterms on 3 November, the US refunding on 4 November, payrolls on 6 November, US CPI on 10 November, the FOMC minutes on 18 November and the second estimate of US GDP on 25 November. Conviction is 2, not 3, because the score is close to the threshold. The opposing factors also share a single trigger: a US-led sell-off or Gulf escalation could make leveraged funds cover a franc short that is the largest since May, while option skew already favours a lower pair. The view would be wrong if payrolls turn negative or risk-off hits US assets first. In either case the score would fall below the threshold through Factors 1 and 3 together.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: Among dollar longs, USD/CHF ranks second tactically, behind only short EUR/USD. The base dossier names it the cleanest bullish dollar expression because it pairs the widest policy gap (387.5bp) with the best carry-to-volatility ratio among the majors (0.59 on implied volatility). Among franc crosses it ranks behind CHF/NOK and AUD/CHF on raw carry, but ahead of them on liquidity. It ranks below CHF/JPY as a funding trade, because the BoJ's possible December hike weakens the yen's funding role but not the franc's. Long USD/CHF is less attractive than long USD/JPY for carry per unit of intervention risk, since Japan-US action caps USD/JPY near 160 and no comparable cap exists here.

strategic.rationale: At strategic weights, Policy & Rates (0.24), External Balance (0.16), Guidance (0.12) and USD Liquidity (0.12) dominate. Rates and liquidity are Neutral, so the signal comes from the structural factors. External Balance subtracts 0.090. The US current account deficit is 3.0% of GDP and its investment position lost USD 1.15tn in a quarter. Switzerland runs a surplus of about 9% of GDP with a real effective rate at a 33-month low, and IMF data show a USD 38.6bn US goods deficit with Switzerland. Guidance subtracts 0.064, because both projection rounds, on 9 and 10 December, lean towards narrowing expectations: the market prices the Fed about 60bp above its median dot, while the SNB has raised its inflation path and stepped back from intervening. Fiscal subtracts 0.039 on the gap between a 6.2%-of-GDP US deficit facing an 11 December funding expiry and a AAA Swiss sovereign. Flows subtract 0.031 on reserve diversification and rising hedge ratios. The net is -0.222: Bearish, conviction 2. The base dossier is Neutral with a bearish tilt on the dollar and the quote dossier mildly Bullish on the franc. Combined, they reinforce a lower pair, because both identify the same December inflection. Bilaterally, the gap that matters is the one not closing: the SNB stays at zero while US deficits widen. The rate factor is Neutral, not Bullish, because the 387.5bp carry is already embedded in a forward that discounts about 4.5% a year of franc appreciation. The edge against pricing is therefore in direction and in the tails rather than in carry. The path of least resistance is firmness into the December decisions, then a grind lower as the Fed's projections confirm a peak and the SNB's forecast edges up. The key dates are the FOMC with projections on 9 December, the SNB assessment on 10 December and the funding expiry on 11 December. Conviction is 2 rather than 3 because the spot view and the forward point the same way: to profit, a short must beat a forward discount of roughly 2.2% over six months. A Fed signalling two more hikes would turn Factors 1 and 6 against this view.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically, short USD/CHF is one of the cleaner expressions of a weaker dollar against surplus currencies. It ranks behind short USD/JPY, where the BoJ's possible December hike narrows the gap, and roughly level with short USD/SEK. On fundamentals it ranks ahead of shorts against deficit currencies such as AUD and NZD. It is the most expensive of those shorts to hold, because the 387.5bp carry is the widest in the set. Among franc longs, the quote dossier prefers short EUR/CHF on fiscal and French-spread grounds. USD/CHF adds the US twin-deficit and guidance channels at a higher carry cost, so it ranks second behind EUR/CHF among strategic franc longs.

strategic.path_expectation: The six-month path is a hump. Through November the pair should follow the tactical staircase towards 0.8340-0.8375 and peak around the 9-10 December decisions, against the five-touch band and the 0.8400 retracement. From mid-December the projection rounds and the 11 December funding deadline start the turn. The first leg breaks the 0.8190 floor and the 100-day near 0.8150 by mid-January, while the falling 200-week reaches 0.8456 and caps any rebound. February and March should grind through the six-touch 0.8016-0.8084 band at about 10-15 pips a week. Rallies should fail at 0.8250-0.8300, and the SNB's 18 March assessment is a step-change risk. By end-April the base case sits at 0.7980, inside the 0.7929-0.8000 band and the 200-day area. A weekly close above 0.8460 at any point means the path has failed. Trade plan (strategic): do not open the short at today's spot. Sell into 0.8300-0.8350 after the 9-10 December decisions, provided the Fed's projections do not lift the 2027 median dot and the SNB's 2027 inflation forecast is at least 0.8%. The alternative is three- to six-month options struck around the forward that pay in the 25% stress tail without paying the carry. Stop on a weekly close above 0.8460, the top of the five-touch band, where the falling 200-week will sit by mid-January. First target 0.8084 (top of the six-touch support), second 0.7980 (inside the second six-touch band). At a 130-pip stop from a 0.8330 entry, a 0.5% risk budget implies notional of about 32% of capital. An options position should use a premium budget of about 0.5% of capital.

risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: In spot terms the distribution favours a lower pair, but carry absorbs almost all of it from today's level. The asymmetry only becomes usable from a higher entry after the December decisions, or through options that pay in the 25% tail without the carry drag.

consensus_divergence.bank_consensus_forecast: MUFG: USD/CHF 0.8480 in Q4 2026, 0.8290 in Q1 2027 and 0.8060 in Q2 2027, as reported secondhand in the Ibani USD/CHF forecast guide (October 2026). No multi-bank survey for this pair could be sourced, so this is a single-bank view, not a consensus.
consensus_divergence.bank_consensus_forecast_source: MUFG bank research, reported secondhand by Ibani (https://www.ibani.com/en/guides/chf-usd-exchange-rate-forecast.md), dated October 2026
consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Bullish over four weeks (score +0.154, conviction 2): carry and the US-Swiss inflation gap support a higher pair until the 9-10 December decisions.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bearish over one to three months (score -0.222, conviction 2): twin US deficits against a Swiss surplus, and December projection rounds that lean towards a narrower expected gap.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: In line on direction: MUFG's path also has the pair firmer into year-end and lower into mid-2027. We place the turn earlier, at the 9-10 December decisions rather than after the fourth quarter.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Directional comparison only. MUFG's fourth-quarter figure implies more near-term dollar strength than our conviction-2 tactical call supports. Its second-quarter 2027 figure implies a decline of about the size the forward already discounts. Additional forecast evidence and magnitudes: MUFG's own forecast page shows the full path 0.8480, 0.8290, 0.8060 and 0.7840, and its latest FX forecast update is dated 1 October 2026. Ibani's 26 October edition noted that the 0.8480 fourth-quarter target now stands 2.9% above the current rate. A dealer-based monthly outlook puts USD/CHF at 0.8226 for November, 0.8200 for December and 0.8417 for January 2027, with an expected November range of 0.8167 to 0.8331. A provider compilation from early August, when spot was near 0.8211, had a Q4 2026 consensus of 0.81180 and Q1 2027 of 0.80800, with USD/CHF showing the greatest provider disagreement, a 12.3% range across 42 providers. That compilation predates the September Fed hike and should be read as stale. In magnitude terms: our tactical 0.8340 sits 140 pips below MUFG's 0.8480 and 114 pips above the 0.8226 November figure. Our end-April 0.7980 sits about 80 pips below MUFG's second-quarter 0.8060 and 78 pips below the six-month forward. The edge over consensus is timing: the turn starts in December rather than after the fourth quarter.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: MUFG's year-end figure treats the franc purely as a funding currency into a Fed hike. We give more weight to two bilateral factors. First, the SNB has dropped its increased willingness to intervene, which removes the backstop that lets carry rebuild unchecked. Second, the 9 and 10 December projection rounds fall within 24 hours and both lean towards a narrower expected differential. We also weigh the US-Swiss external and fiscal gap more heavily over one to three months, so we expect the turn lower to start earlier than a path that peaks in the fourth quarter.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If the turn comes in mid-December, a strategic short entered after the December decisions captures the decline as hedge ratios rise and the franc's surplus reasserts itself. The tactical long earns about 31 pips a month of carry plus a modest drift before then.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If MUFG's stronger year-end path is right and the Fed signals two more hikes, a strategic short pays about 4.5% a year of carry while the pair rises. The tactical long is exposed to a haven-driven franc rally if US-led risk-off arrives before December.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons diverge because the weights move from carry and funding to structure. Tactically, Policy & Rates, Inflation & Growth and USD Liquidity carry 0.53 of the weight and all favour the dollar, with no decision from either bank to interrupt the carry before December. Strategically, External Balance, Guidance and Fiscal carry 0.35 of the weight and all favour the franc. Policy & Rates turns Neutral, because surprise risk at the December projection rounds leans towards a narrower expected gap and the forward already pays for the carry. Where the chart sits against the scored view: we do not think either direction is wrong, but the chart and carry change how each should be traded. The tactical Bullish view meets a stalled chart: lower highs since 14 October and a rejection just under 0.8400. It is supported by a bullish stack, a held 50-day and a twice-defended 0.8190 floor, so the view is tradeable with a tight stop rather than a wide one. The strategic Bearish view runs against a rising 200-day and a pair still at the 84th percentile of its range. Its real support on the chart is the falling 200-week, which merges with the five-touch band in the first quarter. Its real obstacle is the forward. A Bearish score with near-zero expected value after carry at today's spot is the honest description, and that is why the plan waits for December.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: 9-10 December 2026: the FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections on 9 December and the SNB quarterly assessment with its new conditional forecast on 10 December, followed by the US government funding expiry on 11 December.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Express the tactical Bullish view in spot or forwards to collect carry through November, and review or close it ahead of 9 December. Express the strategic Bearish view only after the December rounds confirm a Fed peak and an SNB forecast drift higher, and preferably through options, because an outright short must beat a forward discount of about 2.2% over six months. Level map for the handover: the tactical exit zone of 0.8340-0.8375 is also the preferred strategic entry zone, so the hump has one turning band. If the pair reaches 9 December without trading above 0.8300, the strategic short should be expressed only through options, because the remaining distance to the forward is too small to pay for spot carry.

catalysts.rationale: September CPI was 1.0% with core 0.5%, and the SNB raised its forecast path in September. A print at 1.2% or higher would revive SNB tightening pricing from about 6bp and push the pair lower. A print of 0.8% or lower would confirm the zero rate as a long-run funding anchor and support the pair.

A Democratic House is about 94% priced and a sweep 70%. ING warns a Republican loss of the House could push the administration back towards trade policy, which is dollar-negative. The result also opens the window for possible US strikes on Iran, which would favour the franc's haven role over the dollar.

Treasury plans USD 628bn of fourth-quarter borrowing. Any departure from the promise to hold coupon sizes would lift term premia. In this regime that is more likely to weaken the dollar against a AAA franc through fiscal concern than to strengthen it through yield.

Consensus is +55,000 payrolls and 4.2% unemployment, after a 29,000 September gain with 60,000 of revisions. A negative print would cut December hike pricing and trigger covering of the leveraged-fund franc short, lowering the pair. A print above 100,000 would cement the carry trade.

September core CPI rose 0.3% m/m with a 3.4% three-month annualised pace. A repeat would keep the December Fed hike priced and the US-Swiss inflation gap near 270bp, supporting the pair through the rate differential against a zero-rate SNB. This is the likeliest trigger for a break above the 0.8313 lower high.

The minutes will show how many participants beyond Cook and Hammack favoured a hike. Language such as 'many' or 'most' would lift December odds towards 90% and widen the expected differential with the SNB, which has no communication scheduled before 10 December.

The advance estimate was 3.4% annualised. Revisions are usually small, but a downward revision to consumption would temper the US growth lead over a Swiss economy that SECO expects to grow 1.7% in 2026, weakening the growth side of the differential.

catalysts.event: Swiss Q3 GDP (SECO flash) and month-end dollar funding (week 4 of November)
catalysts.rationale: SECO expects a countertrend after the pharma-driven 1.5% q/q second quarter, so a flat third quarter would push back the 2027 SNB hike option. In the same week, month-end funding with reserves below USD 2.9tn should keep SOFR at or above IORB. Both lean towards a firmer pair in the last week of the tactical window.

catalysts.event: FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.rationale: A 25bp hike to 4.00-4.25% is 77-85% priced and would widen the gap with the SNB to 412.5bp. The projections decide whether the market's path near 4.7% for 2027 survives. A hike with a hold signal is negative for the pair strategically. A hike with higher dots would extend the carry trade.

catalysts.event: SNB quarterly monetary policy assessment with new conditional inflation forecast
catalysts.rationale: The day after the FOMC, the SNB updates a forecast it raised in September to 0.8% for 2027-2028. A further upward drift, or any hint of a 2027 hike, would narrow the expected differential and confirm that the intervention backstop has been withdrawn. That is the strongest franc-positive catalyst on the horizon.

catalysts.event: Expiry of the continuing resolution funding the US government
catalysts.rationale: The stopgap signed on 2 September expires two days after the FOMC, in a lame-duck Congress. A lapse would delay data and raise fiscal risk premia on US assets. Against a AAA franc with debt near 38% of GDP, that is directly negative for the pair.

A BoJ hike would weaken the yen's role as a funding currency further and push more carry funding into francs (affecting both legs via the funding channel). The franc has emerged as a potential successor among carry enthusiasts. More franc-funded carry adds pressure for a higher pair in thin year-end liquidity, even though it deepens the crowding behind the strategic unwind case.

catalysts.event: Year-end dollar funding turn (week 5 of December)
catalysts.rationale: With reserves near USD 2.9tn and the Treasury General Account above USD 1tn, year-end dollar demand should keep SOFR above IORB until the cash balance falls towards USD 850bn. Thin liquidity in the last two weeks of December raises gap risk in both directions.

Bloomberg Economics flags March 2027 as a possible first SNB hike in a high-oil scenario. A move off zero would narrow every differential by 25bp and change the franc's role from funder to normalising currency. It falls just as the falling 200-week reaches the base of the 0.8375-0.8456 resistance band.

assumptions: The price analysis uses daily closing prices for 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30. Spot is 0.82432 at the 30 October close. The valuation date of 1 November is a Sunday, so the gap to the spot date covers only the weekend and no trading session is missing. No weekend-dated sessions appear in the series.
Every level, target, pip distance and percentage in the report is computed against the 0.82432 close; fresher web quotes (for example 0.8250 on 1 November) are not used.

The 50-, 100- and 200-day averages and the 200-week average are simple averages of trading-day closes computed over 4,935 weekday sessions from 2007-11-30 to 2026-10-30. Support and resistance zones are clustered from 1,011 weekly and 463 monthly swing closes over the same history, with touch counts as stated. Zone distances are measured from spot to the zone midpoint.

Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days. ATR(14) is 52 pips. The 52-week percentile is quoted on a closing basis (84th) in the text, with the intraday basis (81st) noted; the 52-week range fields in the structured output use the closing range.
The 200-week convergence timings assume its current slope of -7.7 pips a week continues.
Policy rates are as of 27 October: Fed target mid-point 3.875% and SNB 0%. The 10-year yields of 4.99% (US) and 0.59% (Switzerland) are September monthly averages and are not quoted as live levels.

Implied volatility, risk reversals and butterflies are CME at-the-money quotes on Swiss franc futures options observed 29 October. The three-month tenor is 98.7 days because CME lists quarterly expiries, and the implied-volatility percentile is measured against the range observed since late August, not a full year (the structured percentile of 10 reflects the report's 'bottom decile' wording for one-month implied volatility).

The -448.7bp funding premium is the annualised spread between the December 2026 and March 2027 Swiss franc futures. It is not the policy differential, and forward points derived from it are linear approximations. The structured annualised carry field uses the 387.5bp policy differential, the primary figure in the report; a rolled long earns about 448.7bp.
CFTC franc percentiles cover only the 25 weekly reports since 12 May 2026; the leveraged-fund franc short is the largest in that sample, so the structured percentile is shown as 0.

Bilateral goods trade is IMF DOTS 2024 data as reported in each direction. PPP deviations use World Bank conversion factors and are read as orders of magnitude. No free source publishes three-month CHF/USD cross-currency basis or sovereign CDS.

Default factor weights are applied, and the stance on each horizon follows mechanically from the weighted score. Scenario probabilities are fixed at 50/25/25, and position sizing assumes a risk budget of 0.5% of capital per idea at conviction 2.

Pair-specific chart commentary from web sources is used only for named retracements and dealer levels, never for computed zones. Catalysts dated by week in the report are mapped to the first weekday of that week (2026-11-23 and 2026-12-28).
